questions.question: What is a dental material?
options: A product intended to restore, replace, or treat dental tissues
A manual instrument used for the clinical examination of the oral cavity
An electronic device used to measure pulpal vitality
A medicated solution administered to limit gingival inflammation
questions.explanation: Dental materials encompass all products used for dental reconstruction and therapy.

questions.question: What is the material of choice for direct aesthetic restorations?
options: Light-curing composite resin
Amalgam-based metal alloy
Conventional glass ionomer cement
Cast gold-based precious alloy
questions.explanation: Composite is preferred for its adhesive capacity and its ability to mimic natural tooth shade.

questions.question: What is the main role of mineral fillers in a composite?
options: Improve mechanical strength and reduce polymerization shrinkage
Modify shade saturation for a better rendering
Increase fluidity to facilitate placement
Accelerate the chemical polymerization reaction
questions.explanation: Fillers reinforce the composite structure and limit volumetric contraction.

questions.question: What is the unique biological property of Glass Ionomer Cement (GIC)?
options: Its ability for prolonged release of fluoride ions
Its exceptional resistance to occlusal wear
Its ease of polymerization under blue light
Its excellent translucency similar to enamel
questions.explanation: Fluoride release promotes remineralization and prevents secondary caries.

questions.question: What happens during photopolymerization?
options: Transition from a paste-like to a solid state by light activation
Complete drying of the tooth by a hot, dry air stream
An intense exothermic reaction causing crystallization
The release of residual monomers for better adhesion
questions.explanation: Blue light activates the initiator to transform the liquid resin into a solid polymer.

questions.question: Why is the incremental layering technique used?
options: To reduce stresses related to polymerization shrinkage
To increase the overall speed of the clinical procedure
To simplify the final polishing of the restored surface
To decrease the amount of composite resin needed
questions.explanation: Layering allows better management of the cavity configuration factor.

questions.question: What is the dental adhesive system?
options: A micromechanical bonding interface between tooth and composite
A definitive luting cement for restorations
A metal adhesive intended for fixed prostheses
A protective varnish applied at the end of treatment
questions.explanation: The adhesive system creates the essential union between dental tissues and the resin.

questions.question: What is the standard concentration of phosphoric acid for etching?
options: Approximately 37% by weight
Approximately 10% by weight
Approximately 50% by weight
Approximately 5% by weight
questions.explanation: 37% phosphoric acid gel is the standard for enamel etching.

questions.question: What is the main component of the organic matrix of composites?
options: An organic resin such as Bis-GMA or TEGDMA
A mineral filler based on colloidal silica
A barium glass for radio-opacity
A heavy liquid metal such as mercury
questions.explanation: Bis-GMA is the fundamental organic base of the majority of composites.

questions.question: What is the essential function of the coupling agent (silane)?
options: Chemically bond the fillers to the resin matrix
Modify the shade to better match the tooth
Increase the surface hardness of the final material
Decrease the viscosity of the material before setting
questions.explanation: Silane ensures the bonding interface between the mineral filler and the organic resin.

questions.question: What is a so-called 'flowable' resin?
options: A composite characterized by low viscosity
A pure metallic amalgam without mercury
A definitive cement for prosthetic cementation
A highly radiopaque insulating base
questions.explanation: Their fluidity allows precise adaptation to cavity walls.

questions.question: What is the major environmental risk associated with amalgam?
options: The potential release of mercury into the environment
Rapid corrosion of the restoration margins
Extreme fragility under masticatory stresses
The very high cost of its clinical implementation
questions.explanation: The mercury contained in amalgam is a major toxic pollutant.

questions.question: Which standard defines the biocompatibility of dental materials?
options: International standard ISO 7405
Management standard ISO 9001
The CE marking for European conformity
The French NF quality standard
questions.explanation: ISO 7405 specifies test methods for biological evaluation.

questions.question: What is the hardness of dental enamel?
options: The highest among all tissues in the body
An intermediate value between dentin and bone
A rather low hardness compared to dentin
A hardness equivalent to that of dentin
questions.explanation: Enamel is the most mineralized and hardest substance in the human body.

questions.question: Which material exhibits the best clinical wear resistance?
options: Pressed or milled ceramics
Nanohybrid composite resins
Classic silver amalgams
Hybrid glass ionomer cements
questions.explanation: Ceramics offer superior structural stability and abrasion resistance.

questions.question: What is polymerization shrinkage?
options: The contraction of the material during its setting
Thermal expansion during mastication
The color change after photopolymerization
The loss of adhesion due to poor technique
questions.explanation: Volumetric contraction during setting is inherent to resins.

questions.question: What is an RMGIC material?
options: A glass ionomer cement modified by resin addition
A pure composite with high mineral filler content
A metallic alloy of the restorative amalgam type
A glass ceramic used for veneers
questions.explanation: RMGIC combines the properties of GICs and resins.

questions.question: What is the optimal wavelength for photopolymerization?
options: A spectrum between 440 and 480 nm
A spectrum between 200 and 300 nm
A spectrum between 600 and 700 nm
A spectrum between 900 and 1000 nm
questions.explanation: Blue light (440-480 nm) is necessary to activate the photoinitiator.

questions.question: What is the main effect of etching on enamel?
options: Creation of micro-roughness for adhesion
Complete cleaning of tartar and debris
Polishing of the surface to limit plaque
Aesthetic whitening of the tooth surface
questions.explanation: Etching partially dissolves enamel prisms to create micromechanical retention.

questions.question: What is the risk of an improperly polymerized composite?
options: Post-operative sensitivity and mechanical weakness
A permanent change to a lighter color
A total absence of fluoride release properties
Excessive hardness preventing any adjustment
questions.explanation: Incomplete conversion alters physical properties and biocompatibility.

questions.question: What is the main function of a liner?
options: Ensure pulpal and therapeutic protection
Perform the complete anatomical restoration
Ensure the external sealing of the tooth
Polish the final surface of the filling
questions.explanation: The liner is placed as a thin layer to protect the pulp.

questions.question: Which material is generally the most radiopaque?
options: A composite highly loaded with metals or barium
A pure, unmodified glass ionomer cement
Healthy dentin of the coronary tissues
An unfilled, low-particle flowable resin
questions.explanation: Heavy fillers (barium, strontium) allow the material to be seen on radiographs.

questions.question: What is the C-factor in dentistry?
options: The ratio between bonded and free surfaces of a cavity
The measurement of the total depth of the cavity
The hardness coefficient of restorative materials
The adhesion value of an adhesive system
questions.explanation: A high C-factor means more bonded surfaces, hence more stress.

questions.question: Why is polishing a restoration performed?
options: To reduce plaque retention and improve aesthetics
To increase the overall volume of the restoration
To modify the final shade of the tooth
To strengthen the vitality of the dental pulp
questions.explanation: A smooth surface is less conducive to the development of bacterial biofilm.

questions.question: How does glass ionomer cement bond to the tooth?
options: By a direct acid-base chemical bond
By simple mechanical retention without interaction
Through the use of an intermediate resin-based adhesive
By mechanical friction during placement
questions.explanation: GIC chemically adheres to dental tissues through ion exchange.
